title: KC Mouse-Human Phenotype Browser
bodyHtml:
Most approaches to comparing human and mouse phenotypes rely on matching overlapping clinical or anatomical features. The Mouse to Human Phenotypes Analysis portal takes a different approach: rather than relying on subjective trait descriptions, it leverages statistical enrichment to find mouse phenotypes that share significant associations with human traits. Cross-species relationships are computed using PIGEAN (Priors Inferred from GEne ANnotations), a novel Bayesian method that tests whether genes associated with a mouse phenotype are statistically associated with human phenotypes. This uncovers functional genetic links between species, even when the phenotypic manifestations appear different. This method provides a genetics-first approach to cross-species discovery.

Two modules are available:

1. Mouse to Human Search: For a queried mouse phenotype, identify genetically associated human phenotypes.

2. Human to Mouse Search: For a queried human phenotype, identify genetically associated mouse phenotypes.

PIGEAN jointly tests whether each gene is involved in a human phenotype of interest, given the gene sets that contain the gene (indirect evidence of involvement in a trait) and the GWAS genetic association statistics for variants near the gene (direct evidence of involvement in a trait). Gene sets related to mouse phenotypes are derived from the IMPC/ KOMP2 program. Visit the CFDE Workbench for more information about CFDE-derived gene sets. Phenotypes are derived from common traits in the NHGRI Association to Function Knowledge Portal (A2FKP; n=1,237) and the GWAS Catalog (n=2,213), and from rare phenotypes in Orphanet (n=2,927).

We applied PIGEAN to 6377 total common and rare disease phenotypes/traits, in each case fitting a model using all CFDE mouse gene sets from IMPC/ KOMP2, intersections of CFDE gene sets, and (to increase power) gene sets from the Mouse Genome Informatics database (>11,000 mouse model phenotypes) and MSigDB (pathway analyses). The result of each run is (a) for each mouse phenotype and its corresponding gene set, estimates of the effect of the gene set on the probability that genes in the gene set are involved in human disease, expressed in units of log-odds increase; and (b) for each gene, estimates of the probability that the gene is involved in human disease, expressed in units of log-odds increase relative to the baseline probability 5%. Gene set effects are available either for the gene set in isolation (marginal) or within the joint model (joint), and gene probabilities are available either in total (combined), given only GWAS associations for the gene (direct), and given only gene sets the gene is in (indirect). See our webinar for more details on PIGEAN. Details on an earlier version of the method for gene direct evidence have been published previously (Dornbos et al., 2022).

For each queried phenotype, the top 20 genetically associated phenotypes from the opposite species (human or mouse) are shown. Probability scores are obtained from the following equation: exp(marginal effect + log(background/(1-background))) / (1 + exp(marginal effect + log(background/(1-background)))), where background estimates are 0.05 for common phenotypes and  0.005 for rare phenotypes. Fold-increase scores are the exponential value of the marginal effect.

For the genes within each gene set, direct genetic support scores represent the log of the Human Genetic Evidence (HuGE) scores (Dornbos et al., 2022), which quantify the genetic support for involvement of a gene in one of ~1,200 traits on the Association to Function Knowledge Portal. Combined genetic support is composed of direct support (from GWAS associations near the gene) and indirect support (membership in gene sets with genetic support), expressed as log-odds of probability. Consider the following thresholds for interpreting combined genetic support scores:

  • 1: nominally significant
  • 2: strongly suggestive (i.e., indicative that a gene is in a locus but not yet genome-wide significant)
  • 3: very strong (>50% probability that a gene is involved in the phenotype; similar to nearest gene to a GWAS signal)

See the HuGE Calculator documentation for more details.
